root.note: Arabic qahwa is secure for the drink. Where qahwa itself comes from is disputed, so the story starts there.

history: Coffee reached Europe through the Ottoman Empire. Arabic qahwa became Ottoman Turkish kahve, and Venetian traders, who dealt with Istanbul, brought both the drink and the word to Italy in the 1500s. The Italian spelling caffè has a grave accent on the last vowel, because the stress falls there: you write un caffè, due caffè. In daily life un caffè means a small, strong espresso. For anything else you add a word: caffè lungo, caffè macchiato, caffè americano. Many Italians drink it standing at the counter of a bar. French café and Spanish café come from Italian, while English coffee reached us through Dutch koffie, again from Turkish.
historyEinfach: Caffè comes from Arabic qahwa through Turkish kahve. Venetian merchants brought coffee to Italy in the 1500s. In Italy un caffè means a small espresso. The accent on the last letter shows that the stress is there.

elsewhere.text: English did not take the word from Italian. It came through Dutch, from Turkish. But English has borrowed the Italian words espresso and cappuccino for the types of coffee.
